title: 7 Things in Space So Extreme They Shouldn't Exist

paragraphs: There's a storm on Jupiter so big that Earth would fit inside it. It has been raging since at least the 1800s. And it's only number five on this list.

Because out there are objects so huge, so dense and so violent that they barely seem possible. From a mountain three times taller than Everest, to light that has been travelling for thirteen and a half billion years. These are seven of the most extreme things in the universe.

scenes.name: Olympus Mons
paragraphs: Number seven. Olympus Mons. On Mars, there's a volcano that makes Everest look tiny.
It rises about twenty-five kilometres above the plains around it. That's nearly three Mount Everests stacked on top of each other.
And it's not just tall. Its base is about six hundred kilometres wide, roughly the size of Arizona, and its edges drop away in cliffs up to six kilometres high.
How did it get so big? Mars has no moving tectonic plates. So the volcano sat over the same hot spot, piling up lava again and again, for an incredibly long time.

scenes.name: Saturn's Hexagon
paragraphs: Number six. A storm with straight edges.

Nature almost never makes perfect shapes this big. But at Saturn's north pole, there's a six-sided jet stream about thirty thousand kilometres across. You could line up more than two Earths inside it.
Winds race around it at over three hundred kilometres an hour, with a giant hurricane spinning at the very centre.

The Voyager probes first spotted it in the early 1980s. Decades later, when Cassini arrived, it was still there. Scientists think it forms where winds of different speeds meet and bend the jet stream into waves.

scenes.name: The Great Red Spot
paragraphs: Number five. The Great Red Spot.
This storm on Jupiter is wider than our entire planet. When NASA measured it in 2017, it was about sixteen thousand kilometres across. That's one point three Earths.
But here's the twist. It's shrinking. In the nineteenth century, it was well over two Earths wide.
NASA's Juno spacecraft also found that its roots plunge more than three hundred kilometres down. That's fifty to a hundred times deeper than Earth's oceans.

scenes.name: Neutron Stars
paragraphs: Number four. A sugar cube you could never lift.
When a giant star dies, its core can collapse into a neutron star. Around one and a half times the mass of our Sun, crushed into a ball about the size of a city.
This is the densest material we can directly observe. A piece the size of a sugar cube would weigh about a billion tonnes on Earth. That's as much as a mountain.
And some neutron stars spin hundreds of times every second, sweeping beams of radiation across space like a cosmic lighthouse.

scenes.name: Magnetars
paragraphs: Number three takes that and turns it up. A magnetar.
This is a neutron star with the strongest magnetic field known in the universe. Put one a sixth of the way to the Moon, and it would wipe every credit card on Earth.

On December twenty-seventh, 2004, a magnetar called SGR 1806-20 erupted. It was about fifty thousand light-years away, across the galaxy. And the flash still reached Earth strongly enough to light up our upper atmosphere.
In just a tenth of a second, it released more energy than our Sun gives off in one hundred and fifty thousand years.

scenes.name: M87*
paragraphs: Number two. The first black hole humanity ever photographed.
In 2019, a team linking radio telescopes across the planet, the Event Horizon Telescope, revealed this. The shadow of the black hole at the heart of the galaxy M87.
It's fifty-five million light-years away, and it holds the mass of six and a half billion Suns.
Its event horizon, the point of no return, is just under forty billion kilometres across. Drop it into our solar system, and it would swallow the orbits of every single planet, with room to spare.

scenes.name: MoM-z14
paragraphs: And number one. The most distant galaxy ever confirmed.
It's called MoM-z14, and the James Webb Space Telescope caught its light in 2025. That light has been travelling for about thirteen and a half billion years.
It left this galaxy when the universe was only around two hundred and eighty million years old. That's about two percent of its age today.

So you're not seeing this galaxy as it is now. You're seeing it as a baby, at the dawn of the universe, long before the Sun or the Earth existed. And it's surprisingly bright, brighter than many astronomers expected a galaxy that young could be.
A mountain, a storm, a hexagon, a sugar cube, a flash, a shadow, and a speck of ancient light. Every single one is real.
Which one surprised you the most? Tell us in the comments. And if you want more of the universe at its most extreme, you know what to do.
